title: Thermo-Hydraulic Assessment of a Mountain-Slope Solar Chimney Power Plant with Adiabatic Cooling: Hourly Simulation for Abha, Saudi Arabia
content: Solar chimney power plants are constrained by the maximum chimney height that can be constructed, while mountainous terrain provides additional vertical elevation without increasing the structural tower height. Using twelve months of measured hourly meteorological data from Abha, Saudi Arabia, this study develops a quasi-steady, one-dimensional thermo-hydraulic model of an inclined solar chimney plant that incorporates dry-adiabatic cooling in both the collector and chimney. For a 21.4 km² collector installed on an idealized 12.95° slope with a 1000 m chimney, the predicted annual energy generation is approximately 350 GWh. Neglecting adiabatic cooling leads to an overestimation of annual energy by 37–81%. The model predicts an equivalent flat-ground chimney height of 0.71–0.79 times the terrain elevation gain, although these values may represent upper-bound estimates, as a published CFD study suggests a lower range of 0.32–0.65. Under actual terrain conditions, highly rugged and dissected mountainous areas may restrict the installation of a ground-following solar collector, reducing the estimated annual energy generation to 260–290 GWh. The predicted system performance is primarily influenced by turbine loading, optical efficiency, and the atmospheric temperature lapse rate. The flat-ground formulation predicts a power output of 40–63 kW for the Manzanares prototype, encompassing its reported nominal output of 50 kW without parameter calibration. However, the large-scale inclined configuration remains a model-based prediction that requires experimental validation.
